concept.name: Locate requirement
concept.definition: The Regulation SHO requirement (Rule 203(b)(1)-(2)) that, before effecting a short sale in any equity security, a broker-dealer must have reasonable grounds to believe the security can be borrowed so that it can be delivered on the date delivery is due, and must document that 'locate' before executing the short sale.
concept.intuition: Before you sell shares you don't own, your broker must point to a real, borrowable source of those shares — no selling into thin air.
concept.mechanics: The broker-dealer identifies a source of borrowable shares (its own inventory, a stock-loan desk, or an 'easy to borrow' list) and records the locate prior to the short sale; reliance on blanket assurances without reasonable grounds is prohibited. Bona fide market making is excepted from the locate requirement, though not from close-out and pre-borrow obligations.
concept.failure_modes: Locates are typically arranged before settlement, so located stock can be recalled or used elsewhere by settlement day, producing failures to deliver despite compliance; 'easy to borrow' lists can be stale, and sham locates (e.g., repeatedly relying on the same exhausted source) have been the subject of SEC enforcement.
concept.misconceptions: A locate is not the same as an actual borrow or a guarantee of delivery — it is a reasonable-grounds belief documented in advance; and failing to deliver later is not per se proof the locate was improper, since legitimate delays occur.
concept.example: A trader wants to short 10,000 shares of a small-cap; her broker's loan desk confirms 50,000 shares are borrowable from a lender, records the locate with source and quantity, and only then routes the short-sale order.

citations.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Assistance, Key Points About Regulation SHO
citations.section: Section III: Rule 203(b)(1) and (2) — Locate Requirement
